# KeePass provider test fixtures

None of these open a real vault — every password here is a throwaway
literal that exists only so the test suite can exercise `keepass::filter`'s
tagging rules and `keepass::mod`'s unlock path against real KDBX bytes.

| File | Format | Password | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tagged.kdbx` | KDBX4 / Argon2id | `tagged-fixture-pw` | Generated by this project (see `Phase 2` of the KeePass plan) — 10 entries covering every tagging/dropped-count case: a URL tag, a `context-password` custom-field tag, both on one entry (URL must win), an untagged entry (must not count as dropped), a bad `?os=`, a foreign `?os=`, an empty password, a nested-group entry, an `otp` custom field (`otpauth://totp/Fixture:user9?secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP&issuer=Fixture&digits=6&period=30`), and one entry with a history snapshot. **Only** "Bad OS Entry" (`?os=beos`) and "Foreign OS Entry" (`?os=linux` — deliberately neither of this project's two real CI hosts, mac or win) carry an `?os=` filter at all; every other entry is intentionally OS-unconditional, so `keepass::mod`'s worker-level tests (which filter against the real host OS, not a pinned one the way `keepass::filter`'s own tests do) give the same results on any machine. An earlier version of this fixture accidentally tagged every entry `?os=mac`, which passed here (this project was macOS-only in practice) but silently failed the same tests the moment CI actually ran them on Windows — worth remembering before adding a new tagged entry to this file. |
| `empty.kdbx` | KDBX4 / Argon2id | `empty-fixture-pw` | Generated the same way — zero entries. |
| `legacy.kdbx` | KDBX3 / AES-KDF | `tëst pässwörd 🔑/\` | Copied verbatim from `keepass-core`'s own fixture corpus (`tests/fixtures/keepassxc/kdbx3-minimal.kdbx`, MIT OR Apache-2.0), which we already depend on and vendor via git. One entry, non-ASCII password on purpose. |
| `keyfile.kdbx` + `keyfile.key` | KDBX3 / AES-KDF, password + keyfile | password `tëst pässwörd 🔑/\`, plus the keyfile | Also copied from `keepass-core`'s corpus (`kdbx3-keyfile.kdbx`/`.key`). Since this app deliberately doesn't support keyfile-based unlock, this fixture is what proves the *combined* "wrong password, or this database needs a key file" message — unlocking with the password alone must fail exactly like a wrong password would. |
